name: PCRE2 (PCRE)
workload: Compile three patterns (email, URI, IPv4) and count their non-overlapping matches over a 6.8 MB concatenation of the 'Learn X in Y minutes' docs; elapsed time includes pattern compilation.
claimed_speedup: Default PCRE2 (pcre2_match, interpreter, no JIT): C PCRE2 251.37 ms total (Email 126.10, URI 112.17, IP 13.10) vs C++ STL 1023.49 ms (433.09, 344.74, 245.66), about 4.1x faster (derived from page data). Optimized branch with PCRE2 JIT (pcre2_jit_compile + pcre2_jit_match): C PCRE2 87.87 ms vs C++ STL 1021.10 ms, about 11.6x faster (derived from page data). In the same tables C++ Boost.Regex (104.23 ms) and PHP 8.0.3 (94.33 ms) beat non-JIT PCRE2.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 7.5.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG against PCRE2 10.36-2 (-lpcre2-8); C++ STL: g++ 7.5.0 -std=c++11 -O3 (std::regex); build commands are in run-benchmarks.php; the optimized branch's C file adds pcre2_jit_compile(PCRE2_JIT_COMPLETE) and pcre2_jit_match.
hardware: MacBook Pro (16-inch, 2019), 2.4 GHz Intel Core i9, 32 GB 2667 MHz DDR4, macOS Big Sur 11.2.3; benchmarks run in the repo's Ubuntu 18.04 Docker image
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars (PCRE2 repo); widely embedded (PHP 8 uses PCRE2)
tradeoffs: Backtracking engine with Perl-compatible syntax (lookaround, backreferences, Unicode); worst-case exponential time unless match limits are set (README). JIT matching needs extra executable memory and a JIT stack and is only available on supported CPUs. Syntax and semantics differ from std::regex's ECMAScript grammar, so it is not a drop-in replacement; C API only.
caveats: The seed link pcre.org covers the original PCRE line; this record documents the PCRE2 successor repo, which is the library the linked benchmark measured (PCRE2 10.36-2). The benchmark's own README says 'default settings'; the main-branch C file does not call JIT, so the 4.1x figure is interpreter-only, while the 11.6x figure comes from the 'optimized' branch. Baseline is libstdc++ std::regex from the old g++ 7.5.0 only (no libc++ or MSVC STL). CPU is stated only as '2.4 GHz Intel Core i9' on a MacBook run through Docker for Mac, with no exact SKU. Match counts are printed but not asserted equal across engines. The benchmark repo is archived (January 2026), its last commit is October 2021, and the input text is not a regex-engine stress corpus; PCRE2 is not the fastest engine in the table (Boost.Regex, PHP's JIT build, Rust and Nim beat non-JIT PCRE2). The PCRE2 docs checked (pcre2jit, pcre2perform) carry no numeric speedup claims.

name: protobuf-c
workload: Encode plus decode round trip of one 494-byte protobuf message (all scalar widths, floats, strings, bytes, eight numeric arrays, a nested struct, an array of structs, Unicode strings); each timed iteration re-encodes the freshly decoded message; best of 5 runs; embedded-category host build.
claimed_speedup: protobuf-c 328.0 MB/s (663,929 msg/s) vs nanopb 61.9 MB/s (125,240 msg/s), about 5.3x faster on both metrics (derived from page data). No msgpack comparison found.
compiler_and_flags: Embedded targets are built for size with -Os -flto (README); C compiler and version not stated
tradeoffs: Wire-compatible with Google protobuf, so it needs protoc plus protoc-gen-c and a C runtime; decoded messages are allocated through a pluggable allocator (malloc by default), unlike nanopb's static allocation; the arena README calls it 'desktop-class' and ranks it for reference against footprint-oriented nanopb, so code size is larger than nanopb's.
caveats: Third-party numbers from a rival codec's benchmark arena (SofaBuffers), where protobuf-c is a reference row and not the subject; the author of that arena has an interest in the result. Host CPU, OS and compiler version are not stated, so the run is not reproducible as published (harness code is public). The rows are -Os size-optimized host builds of the embedded codecs, not speed builds, and the 5.3x ratio is derived by comparing two rows of one table. One message shape only. msgpack was not tested in that arena. The GLD.SerializerBenchmark C suite also lists protobuf-c, but its own docs say the protobuf-c row times a shared in-tree proto3 wire codec rather than protobuf-c itself, so it was not used as evidence. No benchmark or performance numbers exist in the protobuf-c README or repo root; issue #394 (nested-message copies) quotes no timings. Last commit April 2025 (release 1.5.2), and the GLD suite author filed a benchmark-fairness request (#803, July 2026) and a spec-compliance report (#810, September 2026) on its issue tracker.

name: Protocol Puffers (protopuf)
baseline: Google protobuf C++ (libprotobuf with protoc-generated classes; version not stated)
workload: Google Benchmark on one small message, Class{name, 3 x Student{id, name}} (45 bytes on the wire): encode into a 64-byte array and decode from a 45-byte buffer, protopuf vs protobuf SerializeToArray / ParseFromArray.
claimed_speedup: Per call: encode 17.2 ns (unsafe_mode) and 29.7 ns (safe_mode) vs protobuf 68.0 ns, about 4.0x and 2.3x faster; decode 188 ns (unsafe_mode) and 217 ns (safe_mode) vs protobuf 244 ns, about 1.30x and 1.12x faster (ratios derived from page data; times from the 'Before' table of PR #53).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the PR; the repo's CMake option ENABLE_BENCHMARK=ON expects a Release build
stars_or_usage: 207 stars; packaged in vcpkg and Conan Center (README badges)
tradeoffs: Messages are described as C++20 template types instead of .proto files (no code generator), so it needs GCC 11+, Clang 12+, MSVC 14.29+ or Apple Clang 17+ and compile times grow with templates; wire format is protobuf-compatible both ways. unsafe_mode skips bounds checks while safe_mode adds out-of-bounds checking and is slower. The README lists the supported field types but no benchmark section.
caveats: Numbers come from a contributor's pull-request comment (PR #53, opened July 2025, still unmerged) and not from the README, docs or CI, and the PR output omits the 'Run on' CPU lines, compiler, flags and protobuf version; the harness source is public (test/benchmark/main.cpp, added in PR #11, January 2021), so a rerun is possible but the published figures are not fully specified. The same PR's decode optimization (145 ns) was not merged because of a length-counting bug, so only the 'Before' figures are used. The message is tiny, and the protobuf decode loop constructs a new pb::Class per iteration (heap allocation for strings and the repeated field). The unsafe_mode rows skip bounds checks, so the headline encode ratio is with checks off; the safe_mode ratios are smaller. The repo README has no benchmark section and the protopuf.surge.sh docs were blocked (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so any numbers there were not seen.
